However, we show that this guarantee, checked one decision at a time, fails over a whole run, because an answer to one permission prompt can rewrite the policy that every later answer is checked against. For example, a remote service with no access to the operator's files approves an unrelated command and attaches an update that deletes the deny rule protecting the project's secrets. The agent then reads the secrets in that session and the next, even inside the vendor's strict sandbox. The root cause is that Claude Code checks only updates that add or replace allow rules. Relays that forward such deletions already exist, including the vendor's own Remote Control. In effect, the right to answer a prompt has become the right to administer the policy. Worse, the deletion leaves the same records as a local edit by the operator, so Claude Code cannot tell who wrote a rule. More generally, what a runtime records decides what it can safely delegate. A runtime that cannot tell who wrote a rule can accept only updates that keep every currently denied call denied, whereas, to protect every party's restrictions, a runtime that records who wrote each rule can let each party remove only the restrictions proven to be its own. We prove that these two bounds are tight. They correctly predict whether the operator's restrictions survive in all thirteen permission designs across ten agent systems, including predictions we wrote down before running Codex, Gemini CLI, opencode, and Goose. Enforcing the bounds at the shared update step blocks the attack. A survey of 2,227 fetched marketplace plugins finds only two that send policy updates.

title: Taylor invertibility and the completion problem for commuting tuples of upper triangular operator matrices
authors: Chafiq Benhida, Hranislav Stanković
abstract: We study commuting $n$-tuples of upper triangular operator matrices $\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{C}} = \bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} \mathbf{A} & \mathbf{C} \\ \mathbf{0} & \mathbf{B} \end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ acting on a direct sum of Banach spaces. Using the long exact sequence in cohomology induced by the Koszul complexes, we show that $\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{C}}$ is Taylor invertible if and only if the connecting homomorphisms $H^k(\mathbf{B}) \to H^{k+1}(\mathbf{A})$ are linear bijections in every degree, and that under natural closed-range hypotheses on the diagonal tuples these bijections are automatically topological isomorphisms. We determine which closed-range properties of the diagonal tuples are forced by the Taylor invertibility of $\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{C}}$ and show by an example that the remaining ones fail in general. We then study the multivariable invertible completion problem, that is, the existence of a coupling tuple $\mathbf{C}$ for which $\mathbf{M}_{\mathbf{C}}$ is Taylor invertible. We reduce it to the realization of a family of cohomological isomorphisms by a single coupling tuple, show that the cohomology of $\mathbf{B}$ and the shifted cohomology of $\mathbf{A}$ must be isomorphic as graded modules over the exterior algebra, and exhibit diagonal tuples whose cohomology spaces are topologically isomorphic in every degree but which admit no Taylor invertible completion, a phenomenon with no one-dimensional counterpart.

title: OVOK: A Recursive Self-Improving Agentic Framework for Video-Based Articulated Robot State Estimation
authors: Cheng Dai, Renkai Luo, Guanfeng Tang, Siming Li, Hao Zhao
abstract: Recovering articulated robot state from video supports metric spatial sensing for manipulation, scene reconstruction, and action planning. Yet the problem is ill-posed: different intrinsics, camera-to-robot poses, and joint angles can explain similar observations. Prior task-specific regressors typically assume known intrinsics, fit one robot through laborious data collection and robot-specific training, and still transfer poorly across scenes. Foundation models apply to any robot zero-shot, but their estimates have large errors. We present OVOK (One Video to Kinetics), a recursive self-improving agentic framework for this task. Under a human-authored protocol, an agentic initializer constructs robot-specific OVOK-4k; a proposer--executor--verifier loop then jointly evolves tools and executable workflows from feedback. Updated tools and workflows are accepted only when the verifier judges a positive improvement. The retained workflow is frozen for accurate inference. Experiments demonstrate that the evolved workflow achieves state-of-the-art results on DREAM-V and RoboKeyGen-V, delivering robust and accurate estimates.

title: Wind-Aware Trajectory Planning for Deformable Aerial Formations
authors: Haozhe Wang, Xun Huang
abstract: Coordinated aerial transport in dense urban environments requires drone formations to navigate confined spaces and adapt to spatially varying winds around buildings. Formation deformation enables passage through narrow spaces but changes individual drone velocities and the local winds they encounter, coupling formation motion with aerodynamic effects. We propose Family-Air, a wind-aware trajectory-family planner that constructs a virtual tube as shared collision-free flight space and jointly optimizes formation-center motion, deformation, and timing. A shared affine transformation represents a continuous trajectory family, incorporating spatially varying wind and deformation-induced velocities into a unified air-relative motion objective. The optimization enforces virtual-tube containment, inter-drone separation, and kinematic feasibility. Simulations across four urban wind-field scenarios demonstrate the importance of local wind-deformation coupling. Flight simulations further show improvements in trajectory tracking accuracy. These results demonstrate the potential of wind-aware trajectory-family planning for coordinated aerial transport in complex urban environments.

title: Spectrality of additive measures with Bernoulli convolutions
authors: Yi-Qiu Mao, Zhi-Yi Wu
abstract: The spectral properties of additive measures of Lebesgue type are by now completely settled \cite{LLP21,ALZ23,KW25,Lu25}. In this paper we continue the study of spectrality for Cantor-type additive measures. For $0<r<1$, let $μ_r$ denote the Bernoulli convolution generated by the maps $x\mapsto rx$ and $x\mapsto r(x+2)$ with equal weights, and consider the Bernoulli-type additive measure \[ μ_{r,s}=\tfrac12(μ_r\timesδ_0+δ_0\timesμ_s). \] For every even integer $R=2k$ we construct an explicit spectrum of the one-dimensional measure $μ_{1/R}$, and from it an explicit spectrum of $μ^{1/R}:=μ_{1/R,1/R}$ lying on the antidiagonal is constructed. Combined with the recently established absence of Fourier frames for the Bernoulli convolutions $μ_{1/N}$ for odd integers $N\geq3$ \cite{DLT26,FSW26}, this yields a parity dichotomy: $μ^{1/R}$ is spectral if and only if $R$ is even. For unequal contraction ratios, we prove that $μ_{1/2,1/4}$ is not spectral. Several open problems and future directions are discussed.

title: On Semilocal Convergence of a Semismooth* Newton Method
authors: Tomáš Roubal
abstract: We give conditions under which the semismooth$^*$ Newton method solves $0\in F(x)$ from a given initial point. At each step, we bound the distance from the corrected point $(x_{k+1},0)$ to the graph of $F$ by a function of the correction length. We also bound $\|A^{-1}B\|$ uniformly over the selected coderivative pairs $(A,B)$. Together, these bounds give a test on the initial graph residual and the radius of a prescribed ball. If the test holds, the iterates converge to a solution in that ball. If the decrease modulus tends to zero, every infinite run converges $q$-superlinearly. For mixed complementarity problems on a box, we assume that the smooth part has a Lipschitz continuous Jacobian and that every nonempty principal submatrix is nonsingular. We bound the error after one step for each regular pair. The bound is quadratic in the distance to a solution and depends explicitly on the norm of the correction matrix. For affine problems, we give a threshold on the norm of the vertical component of a graph point. Below this threshold, all regular pairs at that point give the same solution in one step, even when their rows come from different branches. Hence any run with vanishing graph residuals terminates in finitely many steps. For integer affine data, we give a test for an exact step using only the problem data and the current iterate.

title: RankServe: Rank-Aware CPU-GPU Scheduling for Memory-Constrained MoE Serving
authors: Hengyi Zhu, Zhendong Mi, Pu Zhao, Yanzhi Wang, Hao Wang, Shaoyi Huang
abstract: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models scale model capacity through sparse expert activation, but their large expert pools impose substantial memory requirements during inference. Low-rank compression reduces the memory footprint of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models. However, the heterogeneous expert ranks create unequal storage, transfer, and execution costs. Under limited GPU memory, expert popularity and transfer cost alone cannot determine which experts are most valuable to retain. We present RankServe, a CPU-GPU serving system for compressed MoE checkpoints with fixed expert ranks. Its key insight is to value GPU residency against the cheaper nonresident path, CPU execution or weight transfer followed by GPU execution, under each expert's rank and token load. RankServe aggregates the resulting estimated savings over routing demand and prioritizes experts by savings per byte. It updates residency from recent routing history and selects miss paths using current token loads, allowing temporary GPU execution without cache admission. A variable-rank runtime executes heterogeneous factors through grouped matrix multiplications without common-rank padding. Implemented on vLLM, RankServe is evaluated on three MoE models against six serving systems on a single CPU-GPU platform. Across five batch sizes from 1 to 32, it achieves per-model geometric-mean speedups of $1.69$--$2.29\times$ in time to first token (TTFT) and $1.71$--$2.48\times$ in time per output token (TPOT), relative to the fastest baseline for each configuration and metric.

title: Ada-BFM: Adapting Behavior Foundation Models for Humanoid Scene Interaction
authors: Furui Xu, Weishuai Zeng, Zirui Wang, Kangning Yin, Jiacheng Bao, Huayi Wang, Yingying Qin, Yufei Xue, Yang Tang, Zenghao Tang, Kailin Li, Jingbo Wang, Weinan Zhang
abstract: Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) have emerged as a promising paradigm for general-purpose humanoid control through pretraining on large-scale behavioral data. However, their proficiency in whole-body coordination does not readily extend to scene interaction, which requires adapting motion to scene-dependent geometric constraints and contact dynamics. To bridge this gap, we introduce Ada-BFM, a post-training framework that adapts pretrained BFMs for humanoid scene interaction. Ada-BFM augments the original architecture with a lightweight adapter, enabling interaction-specific adjustments while leveraging pretrained control capabilities. Rather than producing a separate controller for each task, the framework yields a shared model for each interaction domain, supporting diverse tasks involving terrain or object interaction. Extensive experiments in simulation and the real world demonstrate that Ada-BFM enables diverse scene interaction behaviors, accelerates learning compared with training from scratch, and largely preserves pretrained behavioral competence. These findings establish Ada-BFM as an effective and efficient approach to extending the capabilities of BFMs beyond their pretraining settings while retaining their strengths in general whole-body control.

title: Schubert positivity for filtered bundles
authors: Enhan Li
abstract: We characterize formal filtered nefness of a formal quotient flag on a polarized Hodge--Lefschetz module by the formal nefness of its positive-rank total quotients. Using this criterion, we prove that quotient Schubert functors preserve formal nefness and that Schubert incidence modules inherit every commuting formally filtered nef flag. As geometric and numerical consequences, we recover the positivity criteria of Fulton--Lazarsfeld and Fulton and extend the Lorentzian polynomial theorem of Lu and Zheng to derived Schubert classes of filtered bundles. In combinatorics, our framework applies to tautological flags of flag matroids on ordinary and augmented matroid Chow rings as well as on the intersection cohomology of rational projective fans equipped with a common weight map. We deduce concordance-sensitive intersection inequalities, establish the Schubert positivity of the leading Riemann--Roch Chow class of a flag matroid, and show that the nonvanishing supports of derived Schubert numbers on an augmented Chow ring form the Higgs lifts of an intrinsically determined matroid quotient.

title: Upwind finite element approximation of the gradient blow-up time for a viscous Hamilton--Jacobi equation
authors: Yohei Fujishima, Takahiro Yamada
abstract: We analyze an upwind finite element method with piecewise linear elements for a viscous Hamilton--Jacobi equation with a superquadratic gradient source term, subject to homogeneous Dirichlet boundary conditions. On polytopal inner approximations of smooth bounded domains in dimensions $N=1,2,3$, we prove maximum-norm convergence of the numerical solution to the exact solution before gradient blow-up and convergence of gradient-threshold times to the blow-up time under explicit mesh and regularity assumptions. We also verify the regularity assumption and finite-time gradient blow-up for an example on the disk, to which the main theorem therefore applies. Numerical experiments illustrate this gradient blow-up.

title: Prospects for Detecting Post-merger Signals from Binary Neutron Stars with Future Gravitational-Wave Detectors
authors: Jingwang Diao, Teng Zhang, Xingjiang Zhu
abstract: The post-merger (PM) phase of binary neutron star (BNS) mergers carries information about the merger remnant and the dense-matter equation of state, but its observational prospects remain uncertain. We compare two approaches to accessing this emission: the stochastic gravitational-wave background (SGWB) from the BNS population and direct PM-band detections of individually resolved mergers. Using a unified inspiral--merger--post-merger (IPM) waveform prescription and the same astrophysical population model for both calculations, we evaluate representative third-generation detector configurations involving ET, CE, and a dedicated kilohertz detector. For the representative detector networks considered, the baseline IPM model predicts that the all-source, broadband BNS SGWB exceeds the adopted detection threshold across the local merger-rate interval. In contrast, the kilohertz PM-band SGWB remains below this threshold. For individual events, over $R_0=7.6$--$250~{\rm Gpc}^{-3}\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$, the baseline IPM model predicts approximately $5$--$174$ PM-band candidates per year for the dedicated kilohertz detector, whereas the numerical-relativity cases considered here yield approximately $0.07$--$7~{\rm yr}^{-1}$.

title: Start Where the Data Are: Statistical Priors for One-Step Generation on Manifolds
authors: Yuyao Wang, Haoliang Sun, Xiankai Lu, Xinxin Zhang, Yongshun Gong
abstract: Fast generation on manifolds is important for scientific applications such as protein design, yet existing one-step generators often produce spurious samples in low-density gaps between data modes. Our analysis highlights the mismatch between uniform noise and concentrated data, motivating a statistical prior that captures the data's coarse structure. We first estimate this prior by fitting mixtures of tangent-space Gaussians through geometry-aware moment matching. However, independent noise-data pairing can still connect different modes and weaken the benefit of the fitted prior. We therefore introduce posterior coupling, which samples a latent component conditioned on each data point and draws its paired noise from that component. To extend this approach to long torsion-angle chains, where full-covariance mixtures become costly, we use a hidden Markov prior to model sequential dependence with shared parameters. The resulting framework plugs into existing one-step training pipelines while retaining the generator architecture, training objective, and single network evaluation at inference. Experiments on spheres, tori, and SO(3) demonstrate substantial improvements across multiple generators, reducing distributional error by up to $125\times$ and the protein Ramachandran outlier rate from 12.1% to 0.55%.

title: JECT: Addressing the Context Shortcut in Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning for Chest CT
authors: Hanbin Ko, Hong-Jun Choi, Jihun Kim, Young-Gon Kim, Dongheon Lee, Chang Min Park
abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures learn by predicting features of masked regions from visible context. In chest computed tomography, the findings that decide a diagnosis, such as a small nodule, are often not predictable from the surrounding anatomy. A hidden finding is then best predicted toward normal anatomy, and the prediction loss stops rewarding the encoder for representing it. We call this the context shortcut. Conditioning the predictor on the radiology report repairs the prediction, but in our setup the encoder gains little over image-only pretraining: the report supplies what the encoder never had to learn. JECT therefore gives the report two roles: a condition for the predictor and, through masked section-text prediction, a target for the encoder, which must predict the report's anatomical sections from the unmasked scan. A hierarchical three-dimensional encoder that predicts at every stage keeps this clinical content at every scale. In ablations, the text target improves classification and localization, while conditioning adds little to the encoder. Trained from scratch on 173k volumes, the recipe reaches the level of current computed tomography foundation models in classification, retrieval and nodule malignancy, and of task-specific models in lung-cancer risk prediction after fine-tuning. Conditioning still matters: its predictor can be reused, with no extra training, to show where a report sentence acts, changing most at the finding the sentence describes. Code and pretrained weights are available.

title: Spatial switching near a four-loop homoclinic bouquet: a mechanism for multi-bump bound states in coupled nonlinear Schrödinger systems
authors: Sajjad Bakrani
abstract: We study how a localized standing wave of a coupled nonlinear Schrödinger (CNLS) system can switch between components from one pulse to the next. The standing wave reduction of the CNLS system yields a four-dimensional Hamiltonian system with two reflection symmetries, in which four elementary pulses correspond to a bouquet of homoclinic loops to a saddle. For saddle eigenvalues $\pmλ_{1},\pmλ_{2}$ satisfying $0<λ_{1} < λ_{2} < 2λ_1$, and under suitable nondegeneracy assumptions, we construct stable and unstable invariant manifolds of the four-loop bouquet. Apart from trajectories asymptotic to the saddle in the corresponding time direction, these manifolds characterize one-sided trapping near the bouquet within the critical Hamiltonian level, namely the level set containing the saddle equilibrium. Both manifolds have codimension one in this level. We prove that if they intersect transversely away from the bouquet, producing super-homoclinic orbits, then there exist infinitely many multi-bump homoclinic orbits to the saddle. These orbits correspond to multi-bump localized standing waves of the CNLS system.

title: Fluids under tension: dynamics, mechanics, and structure of sparse active adhesive networks
authors: Alex T. Grigas, M. Lisa Manning
abstract: Sparse mechanical networks under tension are inherently prone to gelation/clustering instabilities as bonds break, so they typically cannot reconfigure without collapsing. Subverting this expectation, several biological materials have recently been found to maintain tension and uniformity while flowing. Here, we identify key ingredients needed to generate this fluid under tension and explore how details of the implementation affect ma- terial dynamics, structure, and mechanics. We find that activity must counteract the clustering instability, and that adhesive unbinding must be sufficiently stochastic so that it does not cancel out the activity and drive the system to a quiescent absorbing state. We find that the nature of the activity dramatically changes the material properties and glassy dynamics: self-propelled crawling, implemented as a force monopole, drives collective motion over long wavelengths, resulting in anti-hyperuniform density, whereas a force dipole representing par- ticles pulling on each other drives scale-free collective motion and more uniform density. Both models exhibit exotic mechanics: stresses in each bond relax only through bond turnover, but the global tension never relaxes. In addition, in the crawling model the structure of the network relaxes faster than the pattern of stresses, sug- gesting the material retains a memory of its stress state even as the particle positions reconfigure. Together, this work shows that we can distinguish between activity mechanisms in biological systems by analyzing emergent materials properties, and design exotic emergent properties in reconfigurable active matter systems.

title: A logarithmic saving in the sum-free subset problem
authors: Xiaolu Zhang
abstract: For every sufficiently large $n$ there is a set of $n$ positive integers, all at most $n^2$, whose largest sum-free subset has size at most $n/3+O(n/\log n)$. We bound the number of small divisible elements in a dense set with few Schur triples. A fixed-accuracy cyclic model gives a rotation, and the original integer triple count controls its density at the required scale.

title: Agentic Discovery of Soundness Bugs in Safe Rust Bindings
authors: Marius Momeu, Koushik Sen
abstract: Rust crates confine unsafe code, such as calls into C or C++ libraries or system calls, behind safe interfaces that must uphold Rust's invariants. If an interface encodes one rule of the code beneath it too weakly, a program written in purely safe Rust can cause undefined behavior. Static analyzers and fuzzers are bound to fixed patterns or to the paths they execute. We propose LLM agents as auditors of these interfaces, and study how well they do it. We first define a taxonomy of the defects of such interfaces, including undefined behavior, divergences from the wrapped library, and incomplete unsafe contracts. We then measure, in repeated audits of a real-world crate by a closed and an open model, Claude Opus 5.5 and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, which defect classes agents find, how well they triage them, and what makes them find more. Agents find the first two classes unprompted, but find few incomplete contracts even when asked. Their findings are almost always real, even without an independent reviewer, yet they lack triage discipline: they seldom confirm with a sanitizer, and they stop early. With the same guidance, the open model finds as many defects as the closed one at a quarter of the cost. We integrate these insights in Crustify, an agentic system for automating C-to-Rust tasks, and run it at scale. In 16 widely used crates, including the bindings to the C libraries OpenSSL, SQLite, libgit2, and libcurl and to the C++ engine V8, Crustify found 225 undefined-behavior bugs, 23 behavioral divergences, and 36 incomplete unsafe contracts, between 3 and 61 per crate at a median cost under $50 per audit. In the Linux kernel's Rust abstractions, it found 11 more undefined-behavior bugs and 4 incomplete contracts. Maintainers have fixed 26 of the 83 findings that we reported.

title: Constructive Causal Abstraction and a Case Study in Mechanistic Interpretability
authors: Yuchen Zhu, Sergio Hernan Garrido Mejia, Dominik Janzing
abstract: Existing frameworks in causal abstraction first propose a high-level causal model, and then verify whether its interventional effects agree with those of a given micro-level model - the two models are declared causally consistent when the discrepancy is zero. However, proposing a consistent macro causal model is difficult, because macro causal relations are almost never well-defined, since distinct micro-level interventions associated with the same apparent macro intervention can produce different effects. Our central insight is that causally consistent macro-level models can be obtained constructively: ill-defined macro interventions can be interpreted as missing variables on the macro level, and can be accounted for by introducing a complementary variable q that retains omitted causally relevant state. In the linear case, q has a unique form and we provide sufficient conditions for valid implementations to exist; in the nonlinear case, we provide an ODE-based algorithm for constructing implementations. We call this framework Constructive Causal Abstraction (CCA), and use CCA to formulate the difference between machine-learning model auditing and editing. With the Bias-in-Bios biographies dataset, we demonstrate that CCA allows practitioners to articulate assumptions when detecting the model's gender bias. Finally, CCA resolves a well-known paradox known as "interpretability illusion" which points to a mismatch between the subspace for editing and the one where the model implements a signal-to-output pathway.

title: SciFig2Data: A Workflow for Recovering Structured Data from Scientific Figures
authors: Xinhe Wu, Yicheng Ye, Yadong Jin
abstract: Scientific measurements reported in scholarly articles are often embedded in compound figures rather than available as machine-readable data. Recovering these measurements at literature scale requires an integrated workflow for figure localization, panel decomposition, chart identification, numerical reconstruction, and experimental context association. We present \textit{SciFig2Data}, an automated, high-throughput workflow for harvesting structured experimental data from scientific PDF repositories. The system integrates multi-scale document element detection, adaptive compound figure decomposition, two-stage OCR-based semantic filtering, Swin-based chart classification, and instruction-guided multimodal large language model (MLLM) reconstruction. It further incorporates directory-level batch execution, caching, and structured logging to support large-scale processing. We demonstrate the workflow on two biomedical literature corpora comprising 605 toxicology and pharmacology articles and 551 lipid nanoparticle (LNP) articles. The pipeline successfully reconstructed 468 and 242 tabular outputs from the respective corpora, illustrating its practical applicability to literature-scale scientific data harvesting. By associating reconstructed measurements with caption-derived experimental metadata, SciFig2Data provides a workflow for transforming graphical evidence in scholarly publications into structured, context-enriched data records for downstream AI4Science applications.

title: A Sequential Quadratic Programming Perspective on Optimal Control
authors: Abhijeet, Suman Chakravorty
abstract: This paper investigates the relationship between the iterative Linear Quadratic Regulator (iLQR), Differential Dynamic Programming (DDP), and Newton's method for optimal control problems. Using a unified Sequential Quadratic Programming (SQP) framework, we introduce Newton-LQR, a Riccati-based algorithm that solves for the exact Newton step the optimal control problem. Within this framework, we establish that iLQR is a principled modified SQP method rather than merely an approximation of DDP. We show that iLQR generates a descent direction, whereas the inclusion of dynamics Hessians in DDP and Newton-LQR may lead to indefinite quadratic subproblems and necessitate regularization. We further distinguish DDP and the proposed Newton-LQR algorithm through their treatment of costate information and second-order dynamics terms. Numerical experiments across six benchmark problems demonstrate that iLQR often exhibits superior convergence during the initial optimization phase, while Newton-LQR and DDP can exploit second-order information to accelerate convergence near a solution.

title: Clumping Factor in the Mix: Incomplete Mixing Suppresses Turbulent Reaction Boost
authors: Yu-hsuan Liu, Chia-Yu Hu
abstract: Cosmological simulations often account for unresolved density fluctuations using a sub-grid clumping factor when modeling chemical reactions. To validate this approach, we conduct hydrodynamical simulations of isothermal, supersonic turbulence and track the evolution of passive chemical species in first-, second-, and third-order reactions, exploring seven reaction rates across Mach numbers $M$ = 2-50 in three turbulence driving modes. We parametrize the saturation of clumping factors at $M \gtrsim 10$ due to intermittency (i.e., falling significantly below the log-normal prediction) with a one-parameter fitting formula. Furthermore, we find that the competition between turbulent mixing and the density-dependent reaction rates, governed by the Damköhler number (Da), suppresses the global reaction rate by a \textit{mixing efficiency} factor ($ξ$). For Da $\ll 1$, chemical species remain well mixed ($ξ\to 1$), and the reaction rates are boosted by a clumping factor. For Da $\gg 1$, reactants in dense gas are rapidly depleted before being redistributed by turbulence, causing $ξ$ to drop by a factor of a few to more than an order of magnitude. We quantify the effective mixing efficiency as a function of two dimensionless parameters, $M$ and Da, and provide a fitting formula that can be easily adopted in cosmological simulations to accurately follow unresolved chemical reactions.

title: 10/8-inequality for a spin 4-orbifold with boundary and its application
authors: Masaaki Ue
abstract: As an application of 10/8 inequality for a spin 4-orbifold with boundary, we give criteria of homology 3-spheres represented by certain framed links for having infinite order in the homology cobordism group of homology 3-spheres. Such a class of homology 3-spheres includes certain plumbed 3-manifolds, 1/odd surgeries along certain knots with many twists, for example, certain Montesinos knots, $(p,q)$ cable knots of any knot with some large $p$, $q$, etc.

title: BODYBENCH: Evaluating Adversarial Image Defenses Against AI Nudification Inpainting
authors: Li Qiwei, Salma Abdel Magid, Olga Russakovsky, Eric Gilbert, Sarita Schoenebeck
abstract: Adversarial perturbation defenses protect images from unauthorized edits by adding imperceptible noise. Yet none of these methods have been evaluated against nudification, despite AI-generated non-consensual intimate imagery (AIG-NCII) being among the most documented harms of generative AI. Moreover, nudification edits are readily carried out through inpainting, the primary setting these protection methods are designed to defend against. We argue this is a problem-formulation failure since prior threat models do not correspond to nudification edits (also called attacks). The misalignment of existing approaches is structural, spanning mask shape, training and testing prompt distributions, and success criterion which causes existing evaluations to systematically overestimate protection effectiveness. We reformulate image protection against unauthorized editing around this documented harm. We introduce BODYBENCH, a benchmark of 648 fully synthetic clothed adult subjects, each paired with 11 mask variants spanning body, face, and context regions. We propose three harm-aligned metrics: sexualization, naturalness, and recognizability that jointly determine whether an inpainted output constitutes a successful nudification attack. Auditing four recent protection methods (PhotoGuard, DiffusionGuard, AdvPaint, DiffVax) on BODYBENCH, we find that protection succeeds in only one configuration of one method, and only under exact mask alignment between defender and attacker---a condition no real defender can guarantee and one that we show is easily always bypassed. We also show that standard evaluation metrics such as peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) are essentially uncorrelated with nudification protection. BODYBENCH makes this misalignment measurable and provides a foundation for defenses grounded in documented harm.

title: Symmetry-constrained order hierarchy of connected optical responses in a five-level Rydberg-EIT medium
authors: Lintian Luo, Weixuan Gu, Yan Li
abstract: Determining the connected many-body correlations required for a nonlinear optical response of a given order is a central challenge in interacting open quantum systems. We establish a symmetrybased selection rule for connected optical responses in a driven-dissipative Rydberg-EIT model. Under the specified Lindblad conditions, local phase covariance and zero-probe factorization imply that an n-atom connected contribution to the root optical coherence is forbidden below probe-amplitude order 2n-1. Consequently, optical-response coefficients through fifth order involve at most three-atom connected clusters, without assuming weak interatomic interactions. Direct finite-cluster calculations confirm the predicted lowest allowed orders, while an illustrative Maxwell-propagation calculation shows that triplet contributions can partially oppose pair-induced polarization rotation. Our results establish a rigorous connection between optical perturbation order and the connected many-body sectors that can contribute to it.

title: The effects of closure parameter on the properties of kinetic range plasma turbulence
authors: Jago V. H. Edyvean, Andrea F. Irwin, Tulasi N. Parashar
abstract: Simulations of plasmas such as the solar wind require an accurate representation of kinetic physics given the lack of frequent collisions. Fully kinetic treatments are computationally expensive and necessarily confine simulations to small domain sizes. A good compromise is to utilise higher-order fluid-moment models such as the 10-moment model. This model retains all physics up to the second moment, with the moment hierarchy closed by approximating the heat flux. One choice is to use a model for the divergence of the heat flux, $\partial_m q_{ijm} \approx v_t |k_0|(\mathbf{P}_{ij}-pδ_{ij})$, with a free parameter $k_0$, called the ``closure parameter''. We study the effects of this closure parameter on the properties of turbulence, combined with artificial ion-electron mass ratios. We show that the heating of the two plasma species is affected by the choice of the closure parameter. For all combinations of closure parameters, the relative compressive and incompressive heating rates are affected even for realistic mass ratios. The effects are more prominent for lower mass ratios and diminish when approaching realistic mass ratios.

title: Beyond the Thermodynamic-Volume Limit in Holographic Complexity
authors: Di Wu, Robert B. Mann
abstract: In the large black hole regime, holographic complexity obeys a thermodynamic-volume scaling law, while the finite-size approach to this limit remains unresolved. In this Letter, we develop an analytic description of finite-size corrections to this scaling for complexity of formation in the complexity=volume (CV) proposal of odd-dimensional equal-spinning Myers-Perry-AdS black holes. We find that the leading finite-size correction retains state dependence that is absent from the limiting thermodynamic-volume law. This correction changes sign at a distinguished Critical Horizon Ratio (CHR), where the generic leading finite-size contribution vanishes and convergence to the thermodynamic-volume law is correspondingly accelerated. We further determine the dimension dependence of the CHR analytically, showing that it approaches a finite nonextremal value at large dimension with a calculable leading finite-dimensional correction. These results show that the finite-size approach can provide a new probe of holographic structure, motivating its exploration across different realizations of holographic complexity and its eventual characterization in the dual field theory.

title: BEARING: Who Is Talking to Whom? Grounding Acoustic Direction in Vision for Online Multi-Party Conversation
authors: Nader Lobandi, Lombe Chileshe, Mohammad Mehdi Hosseini, Mohammad H. Mahoor
abstract: Understanding a group conversation means deciding, from video and audio, who is speaking and to whom. Leading systems treat these tasks offline on single-channel clips and align models with a self-evaluation reward. We propose BEARING, a geometry-first alternative built on one measured signal: the direction from which a microphone array beside the camera hears a sound. A label-free calibration learned from the stream registers this direction into the camera image, and an online registry of faces, voices and directions needs no enrollment. The registered direction serves as (i) a visual prompt for a vision-language model, a marker on the speaker or an arrow toward an off-screen source; (ii) one input of a reliability-weighted fusion with visual active-speaker detection, for speakers in the same direction from the array; and (iii) a verifiable reward for alignment: the named speaker must sit where the sound comes from, the confidence must match that check, and always answering "group" earns nothing. Every decision is online, with the lookahead as an explicit parameter. On 9,498 addressee-labelled utterances from three AMI sites and egocentric EasyCom, the direction prompt raises speaker accuracy from 54% to 74%; addressee accuracy moves by about two points, because telling one addressee from the group depends on the words more than on where people are. For co-located speakers on AVDIAR, visual active-speaker detection holds 95% where direction alone falls to 59%. The verifiable reward beats self-evaluation under GRPO, reward-ranked fine-tuning and DPO; shrinking the lookahead from 5 s to 0.5 s costs 4.5 DER points on AMI, and learning the registration online costs a dip in the first two minutes before the system overtakes vision alone. Code and evaluation protocols will be released.

title: Geo-SMILE: Statistical Model-Agnostic Interpretability with Local Explanations for Geospatial Machine Learning
authors: Shadieh Mohammadi, Koorosh Aslansefat
abstract: Conventional post-hoc explanation methods were developed largely for non-spatial inputs and often provide limited explicit treatment of geographic context. We introduce Geo-SMILE, a model-agnostic framework that distinguishes substantive Feature explanation from geographic-position response through complementary perturbation branches. The Feature branch masks substantive predictors while retaining observed coordinates; the Geo branch relocates geographic units while holding substantive predictors fixed. Following the statistical-distance-weighted surrogate principle of SMILE, input-distribution Wasserstein distances determine coalition locality weights and weighted Ridge surrogates approximate expected black-box predictions. GeoSensitivity, signed in the keep orientation, quantifies fitted-model responses to geographic-player relocation under the specified design. Across crime prediction in Hull, housing-price prediction in Seattle and ride-hailing demand in Chicago, held-out weighted surrogate fidelity ranges from $R_w^2=0.910$ to $0.989$ in the Feature branch and from $0.842$ to $0.906$ in the Geo branch. The framework makes geographic position an explicit object of post-hoc explanation while requiring separate assessment of interpretation, stability and reference dependence.

title: Unit Lattices of Totally Complex, non-CM $D_4$-Octic Number Fields
authors: Sara Chari, Kelly O'Connor
abstract: Given a number field, we can endow the unit group of its ring of integers, modulo torsion, with the structure of a lattice. Included in the study of the distributions of these lattices is the classification of shapes of unit lattices arising from $D_4$-quartic number fields with signature $(2,1)$. We extend this work to rank 3, by investigating the shapes of lattices arising from the unit groups of totally complex, non-CM $D_4$-octic number fields. In particular, we show all such unit lattices have automorphism group $D_4\times \mathbb{Z}/2{\mathbb{Z}}$, yet none correspond to Gram matrices whose entries are all algebraic.

title: A mixed-primal FEM for Poisson-Fermi interfacial problems
authors: Siyad Rahman Mandottil, Neela Nataraj, Ricardo Ruiz-Baier
abstract: This paper presents a mixed-primal FEM for a linearised Poisson--Fermi interface problem arising from the Bazant--Storey--Kornyshev theory, which describes electrostatic interactions in ionic solutions. It leads to a transmission problem coupling a fourth-order equation in the solvent region with a second-order equation in the solute region. To precisely compute the electrostatic stress and the interactive force in the electrolyte, we reformulate the fourth-order problem as a mixed system by introducing the gradient of the electrostatic potential, the divergence of its gradient, and the gradient of its divergence as additional independent variables. The second-order problem is studied in its primal form as this approach eliminates the requirement for Lagrange multipliers to enforce the transmission conditions. The resulting formulation is discretised using Raviart--Thomas finite elements for the vector variables and piecewise polynomial finite elements for the scalar variables. Well-posedness of the mixed-primal formulation and optimal a priori error estimates for the field variables as well as for the postprocessed Maxwell tensor are established under suitable regularity assumptions, in parameter-weighted norms in which the inf-sup constant is independent of the correlation length and of the permittivity ratio. The constants in the error estimates are independent of both parameters as well, up to a loss of at most half an order when the mesh does not resolve the length scale (square root of the relative permittivity); the Sobolev norms of the solution may still depend on the parameters through boundary layers. The postprocessed Maxwell stress converges with optimal order on quasi-uniform meshes, except for the lowest-order scheme in 3D. Numerical experiments validate the theoretical convergence rates and demonstrate the properties of the proposed method for problems in 2D and 3D.

title: Meta-Amortized Cognitive Modeling
authors: Jerry M. Huang, Lukas Schumacher, Niek Stevenson, Mischa von Krause, Stefan T. Radev
abstract: Cognitive modeling is highly iterative. Researchers repeatedly revise model structures, parameterizations, covariates, and experimental designs as theories evolve and data accumulates. Amortized Bayesian inference with neural networks provides rapid estimation for individual models, but every revision requires new simulations and training. Here, we introduce CogFormerV2, a meta-amortized framework that enables researchers to specify, revise, and fit cognitive models with a single network, carrying amortization across an entire space of models all at once. Trained once in about a day on a single GPU, it delivers accurate, well-calibrated posteriors across more than 14.6 billion model configurations spanning binary, multi-alternative, and continuous decisions, with varying parameter sets, covariate structures, trial counts, and contamination levels. It can fit empirical data from distinct behavioral tasks and extends to new models through continual learning and representation transfer. Released as an open-source interactive application, CogFormerV2 provides a reusable infrastructure for meta-amortized inference in cognitive modeling, while carrying the potential to accelerate computational modeling workflows at large.

title: Uniform stabilization of degenerate thermoelasticity with non-autonomous conductivities
authors: Menglan Liao
abstract: We study a one-dimensional thermoelastic system with space- and time-dependent conductivity vanishing at one endpoint, under Dirichlet or zero-flux thermal conditions. Uniform comparison with the initial conductivity and local temporal regularity yield global well-posedness for energy data. A quadratic lower bound ensures uniform exponential decay for every fixed coupling $κ>0$, with constants depending only on $κ$ and uniform spatial bounds, independently of the starting time and local temporal regularity norms. This includes the critical conductivity $a=x^2$ with noncompact thermal embedding. For autonomous powers $a=x^α$ with the corresponding boundary realizations, exponential stability holds uniformly in $α$ for $0<α\le2$. For $α>2$, concentrating approximate equilibria show that the semigroup norm equals $1$ at every time and preclude uniform decay even from the generator graph domain to the energy space. Proofs combine a common-domain construction, interior-average compensation and time averaging for Dirichlet conditions, and a strict Lyapunov functional for zero-flux conditions.

title: Turnpike Estimates and Limiting Behavior for $N$-Player Differential Games under Displacement Monotonicity
authors: Asaf Cohen, Antonios Zitridis
abstract: We study the long-time behavior of open-loop Nash equilibria of $N$-player stochastic differential games with nondegenerate idiosyncratic noise, under displacement monotonicity of the costs and joint strong convexity of the Lagrangians. We prove an exponential turnpike estimate: as the remaining horizon grows, the decoupling fields of the finite-horizon Pontryagin systems converge exponentially fast to the solution of a stationary Pontryagin system, which is unique in a natural stability class, and on bounded time intervals the equilibrium states and controls converge to those generated by this solution. The limiting control is a strong open-loop equilibrium of an associated ergodic $N$-player game, and the ergodic constant $λ^{i,N}$ of each player is the same at every such equilibrium. For the finite-horizon game, the law of the equilibrium state, at times away from the initial and terminal times, is exponentially close in the Wasserstein distance $W_2$ to the invariant measure of the limiting dynamics. Finally, the equilibrium cost of player $i$ on $[t,T]$ equals $(T-t)λ^{i,N}$ plus a uniquely determined corrector, up to an error exponentially small in $T-t$.

title: Coherent meson-baryon conversion in a cold-atom non-Abelian lattice gauge simulator
authors: Tian-Yi Wang, Wei-Yong Zhang, Tie-Jin Zhong, Ming-Gen He, Zhao-Yu Zhou, Hui Sun, Zhen-Sheng Yuan, Jian-Wei Pan
abstract: Quantum chromodynamics (QCD), the non-Abelian gauge theory of quarks and gluons, provides a microscopic description of strongly interacting matter, including hadron structure and dynamics. Real-time dynamics and finite-density properties of these systems remain challenging for conventional Monte Carlo methods because of sign problems. Quantum simulation provides a complementary approach, although circuit depth and noise limit digital implementations and non-Abelian gauge-matter interactions remain difficult to engineer in analog systems. Here we realize a non-Abelian lattice gauge model with dynamical matter in an analog cold-atom simulator and directly observe its hadronic dynamics using site- and spin-resolved quantum gas microscopy. This realization is enabled by harnessing two hyperfine states and site-occupation configurations of 87Rb atoms to jointly encode both matter and gauge fields. We tailor resonant tunneling in a spin-dependent optical superlattice to implement a gauge sector of a truncated one-dimensional SU(2) quantum link model with independently tunable mass and gauge coupling. Leveraging this control, we track the conversion of an initially mesonic state into baryonic or vacuum-like configurations through slow mass ramps. Near resonance, we observe coherent oscillations between mesons and baryon-antibaryon pairs and characterize the conversion efficiency as a function of mass, gauge coupling and net baryon density. Our realization establishes an atomic platform for non-Abelian gauge dynamics, opening a route to microscopic studies of nonequilibrium dynamics in strongly interacting matter.

title: topAC99: A compact MATLAB implementation of filter-free Allen--Cahn topology optimization with matrix-free field transfer
authors: Run Du
abstract: This paper presents topAC99, a self-contained, toolbox-free 99-line MATLAB kernel for filter-free Allen--Cahn topology optimization via the Augmented Lagrangian method on structured quadrilateral meshes. The software architecture combines three compact numerical components: (i) a lumped nodal discretization with a 7-line Kronecker-sum 5-point Laplacian that enforces homogeneous Neumann conditions at width-invariant sparse memory cost; (ii) matrix-free node-to-element averaging and adjoint backpropagation via two-dimensional convolutions (conv2); and (iii) an inlined 18-line 1D-dual bisection Method of Moving Asymptotes (MMA) solver for signed sensitivities. Benchmarks from 60x40 to 300x200 meshes (121,002 degrees of freedom) against convolution- and PDE-filtered SIMP baselines show that Allen--Cahn residual and adjoint evaluations add only 0.7%--1.2% per-step overhead while converging in 78--92 iterations on fine grids. Minimal-line extensions to a symmetric force inverter compliant mechanism and a passive-deck highway arch bridge further demonstrate the versatility of the 99-line kernel.

title: TDD: Target-Discrepancy Distillation for Underwater Image Enhancement
authors: Zefan Feng, Zhaocheng Yu, Laibin Chang, Kui Jiang, Junjun Jiang, Xiaopeng Fan
abstract: Underwater degradation changes image appearance and can compromise the semantic cues used to guide enhancement. Identifying scene content alone does not explicitly specify the appearance to recover or the input-dependent changes associated with that target. We propose target-discrepancy knowledge distillation (TDD) for underwater image enhancement, which organizes guidance around these two aspects of the same restoration problem. For each degraded-reference training pair, reference features from an underwater vision-language teacher provide target-appearance supervision, while paired feature residuals describe the observation's discrepancy relative to the same target. Both representations are jointly distilled into a lightweight guidance network that predicts them from the degraded image alone; neither the teacher nor reference images are required at inference. To align their use with their supervisory roles, we introduce progressive knowledge fusion within a multi-scale enhancement network. The estimated discrepancy first conditions spatial feature updates, after which target-appearance guidance refines the updated features and channel interactions consolidate their responses. This correction-before-refinement design lets target-guided refinement build on discrepancy-conditioned features. Experiments on six underwater benchmarks demonstrate competitive performance across full-reference and no-reference metrics. Ablations and feature visualizations analyze the contributions of the knowledge source, joint distillation, and progressive fusion.

title: A sharp form of Welsh's log-concavity inequality for chromatic polynomials
authors: Meiqiao Zhang, Fengming Dong
abstract: Let $G$ be a simple graph of order $n\ge 1$, and let $P_G(x)$ be its chromatic polynomial. In the early 1970s, Welsh conjectured that $P_G(k)^2 \ge P_G(k-1)P_G(k+1)$ holds for any positive integer $k$. This conjecture was also independently proposed by Brenti in 1992, while in 1997, Seymour disproved it for $k=6$ by constructing an infinite family of graphs of sufficiently large order as counterexamples. In 2005, Dong, Koh and Teo conjectured that $P_G(x)^2 \ge P_G(x-1)P_G(x+1)$ holds for all real $x\ge n$. In this paper, we prove that the inequality holds for all real $x\ge n-1$. Equality holds if and only if $n\ge 2$, $G$ is complete, and $x=n-1$. Moreover, the bound $x\ge n-1$ is best possible for every $n\ge 2$.

title: Gamification in the age of AI: surveying player perceptions of motivation, manipulation, and data protection
authors: Kurt Horvath, Tom Tucek
abstract: Modern games and applications increasingly employ artificial intelligence (AI), user modeling, and gamification to influence user behavior, sustain engagement, and monetize attention. Although these mechanisms can enhance motivation and enjoyment, they also raise concerns about manipulation, personal data usage, and transparency. To examine how players perceive these dynamics, we conducted a survey with 28 adult participants. Respondents expressed strong concerns about the collection and exploitation of personal information in games and gamified applications, while also reporting low awareness and a limited sense of control over how their data is used. They evaluated progression features such as leveling systems and leaderboards as motivating. In contrast, they rated retention-focused mechanics such as daily login rewards and random reward reveals as highly manipulative. Participants reported that these systems can create fear of missing out or resemble gambling. Participants also expressed support for regulatory measures that limit exploitative design and protect vulnerable users. These findings reveal a clear gap between increasingly powerful engagement strategies and user trust, illustrating the need for more responsible and transparent gamification practices.

title: Machine Learning-Based Quantum Error Mitigation for Bound-State Simulations
authors: Sumit Choudhary, Tarunpreet Kaur, Harjeet Kaur, Harpreet Singh
abstract: Noise in quantum devices remains a major challenge for reliable quantum simulations, making quantum error mitigation an important tool for improving their accuracy. Machine learning-based quantum error mitigation (ML-QEM) provides a useful approach, but its performance depends on the training datasets and may produce reconstructed quantum states that are not physically valid. In this work, we introduce an ML-QEM framework that uses residual learning with convex projection to ensure that reconstructed density matrices satisfy physically valid density matrices. We study the effect of different training datasets and regression models using Haar-random and variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) ansatz states. We compare the proposed approach with conventional ML-QEM, readout error mitigation, and zero-noise extrapolation. The method is tested on IBM quantum hardware for three- and four-qubit simulations of the bound $Λ$-deuteron and $Λ$-$α$ hypernuclear systems, respectively. For the three-qubit system, ridge regression trained on VQE-ansatz states gives a ground-state energy of -0.134 MeV, close to the ideal value of -0.135 MeV, with a state fidelity of 0.999. For four-qubit system, kernel ridge regression gives ground-state energies of -3.014 and -3.045 MeV, with corresponding state fidelities of 0.995 and 0.998. These results show that physically constrained reconstruction, along with the choice of training datasets and regression models, can improve ML-QEM performance for the quantum simulations studied in this work.

title: VividAudio: Multi-Event Reference-Conditioned Video-to-Audio Generation
authors: You Li, Dewei Zhou, Fan Ma, Dongliang He, Yi Yang
abstract: Existing video-to-audio (V2A) methods have achieved promising results in synthesizing high-quality audios. However, as V2A advances toward more flexible user-directed creation, existing methods remain notably limited in controlling the distinct acoustic identities of multiple events within a video. We therefore formulate multi-event reference-conditioned V2A (Mr-V2A), where each event is assigned a specific audio reference and target time span. Mr-V2A presents three key challenges. First, event-level reference-target training pairs are scarce. We introduce Intra-Video Event Variation (IntraEvtVar), which constructs non-oracle pairs through four variation modes of events mined within each video. Second, we organize the references into a Time-Aligned COmposite Reference (TACO-Ref) and inject it through local and global pathways: the local pathway retains time-resolved event cues, while an Audio Q-Former provides a clip-level acoustic-context condition. Third, jointly conditioning on multiple references can cause acoustic-attribute leakage across events. Localized reference attention and the TACO-Ref Router (TRR) explicitly constrain event-to-reference correspondence to reduce such interference. Experiments on VGGSound-Ref and VividBench demonstrate stronger reference controllability than existing V2A and exemplar-based methods while maintaining competitive Foley generation quality.

title: Phoneme-identity depth profiles do not reliably predict LoRA placement for dysarthric ASR
authors: Bernard Muller, LaVonne Roberts
abstract: Parameter-efficient adaptation of a speech foundation model to dysarthric speech requires a rarely justified choice: which encoder layers to adapt. A recently proposed strategy is to probe the encoder, find where phonetic information becomes most decodable, and put the adapters there. We test that inference across two ASR models (Qwen3-ASR, Whisper-small) and two dysarthric corpora (Mandarin CDSD, English UASpeech), holding recipe and seed discipline constant. The inference fails. Measured under one pipeline rather than inherited from published figures, all four phoneme-error curves minimise between 83% and 92% of relative depth, each model's minimising layer moving no further between corpora than between probe seeds. The best adaptation band is not similarly constant: none of three natural mappings from the curve to a band -- steepest improvement, lowest band-mean error, or knee location -- recovers the best tested configuration. We do not claim no statistic of the curve could work, only that these three do not. Placement still matters, but is model- and corpus-specific. On CDSD the models disagree -- Qwen3-ASR prefers its upper third (29.88% CER, three-seed mean), Whisper-small all-block LoRA (53.56%) -- while on UASpeech neither favours the upper band. At three seeds, upper-versus-all is resolved (-1.31 pp, CI [-2.16, -0.25]) but upper-versus-middle is not (-0.83 pp, CI [-2.06, +1.86]). The two models' preferences differ as a directly tested interaction (-4.71 pp, CI [-6.17, -2.89]); we designate this the primary claim, and record that the designation was made post hoc. On Qwen3-ASR x UASpeech, adapting near the input is reliably worse than not adapting at all (+9.90 pp CER). We recommend choosing the band by a short adaptation sweep on the model and corpus in hand, not by reading it off a probe.

title: Overparameterized Simulation-Error Minimization for Nonlinear System Identification: Horizon-Uniform Landscape and Identifiability
authors: Cesare Donati, Constantino Lagoa
abstract: Simulation-error minimization is a standard criterion in nonlinear system identification, but its landscape is nonconvex and its conditioning can degrade geometrically with the data horizon N. We propose to lift the trajectory with a free, softly penalized per-step correction, which yields a fit loss that gradient descent provably minimizes: under a rank condition on the output map and a bound on the one-step Jacobian, it satisfies a Polyak-Lojasiewicz inequality with an explicit constant independent of N. A zero-loss model leaves the physical parameter undetermined. Identifiability is restored by a minimal-correction selection principle: under structural identifiability, the global minimizer of the penalized loss returns the true parameters for every positive penalty weight, and under noise and unmodeled dynamics the parameter error grows at most linearly with the mismatch. The resulting estimator, gradient descent on the fit loss followed by a homotopy in the penalty weight, reconciles fit and selection, with a local convergence guarantee. In experiments, it recovers the parameters on long records of expanding and chaotic systems on which single shooting fails.

title: Cross-Order Information-Guided Estimation for Non-Uniform Hypergraphs
authors: Rongzhuo Nie, Menghao Wang, Sanguo Zhang, Mingyang Ren, Guojun Zhu
abstract: Many real-world interactions involve groups of nodes rather than pairs. A non-uniform hypergraph records such interactions as hyperedges of different orders, where the order counts the nodes in a hyperedge. Full estimation evaluates every candidate hyperedge, whose number grows exponentially with the order, and classical remedies sacrifice higher-order information or aggravate computation. The orders are not isolated: the lower orders, cheap to compute and rich in information, reveal where higher-order hyperedges are likely to occur. We propose CINE (Cross-order Information-guided Negative-sampling Estimation) under a latent space model in which all orders share latent positions. Starting from order two, CINE climbs one order at a time. At each higher order, CINE keeps all present hyperedges, samples a small subset of negative examples guided by lower-order scores, and corrects for the known inclusion probabilities to preserve the target of full estimation. CINE thereby lets users choose the trade-off between computation time and estimation accuracy: the retained orders and the sampling budget set the time, and the retained information provably approaches full-data information as the sampling budget grows. In simulations, CINE approaches the accuracy of full estimation at a small fraction of its computation time, and larger teams in MADStat reveal research associations.

title: Stability and periodic switching in feedback systems with sector-bounded hybrid integrators
authors: Sebastiaan van den Eijnden, Kai Wulff, Christoph Weise, Johann Reger
abstract: We study stability of piecewise linear systems composed of the feedback interconnection of a linear time-invariant process and a sector-bounded hybrid integrator. Exploiting the observation that for such systems state-dependent switching sequences asymptotically exhibit periodic behaviour, we develop a spectral approach to stability analysis as an alternative to sufficient Lyapunov-based methods. We formulate a conjecture that asymptotic periodicity holds irrespective of the initial conditions and system stability, and provide a description of the limit system and propose an algorithm to obtain its parameters. We establish this rigorously for second-order linear-time invariant processes. Based on spectral properties of the resulting periodic limit system, we derive sufficient stability conditions. The results provide a novel viewpoint for accurate stability analysis of general state-based piecewise linear systems.

title: The polygonal Steklov--Weinstock inequality
authors: Zhuo Cheng, Yian Zhang
abstract: We prove that for every integer $N \ge 3$, the regular $N$-gon uniquely maximizes the scale-invariant first positive Steklov eigenvalue $L(P)σ_1(P)$ among all simple planar polygons $P$ of positive area with at most $N$ sides, up to similarity (and up to congruence at prescribed perimeter). Our proof combines two complementary realizations of the Rayleigh--Ritz variational principle. For convex competitors, we transplant a first Steklov eigenfunction of the regular reference polygon: for triangles, affine transplantation aligned with a longest side yields both the sharp inequality and a two-sided linear stability bound in terms of the maximal side-length deviation; for convex $N$-gons with $N \ge 4$, a piecewise harmonic fan transplantation across radial sectors matches traces along the internal seams. In the quadrilateral case, centering the fan at the vertex average pairs opposite sides and controls the displacement of the diagonal midpoints, whereas for $N=5$ the spectral deficit dominates both the area deficit and the squared vertex and Hausdorff distances to the regular pentagon. Nonconvex competitors are treated by stratifying them according to their number $p \le N-1$ of strictly convex corners: boundary moment inequalities handle $p=3$, while conformal disk tests localized on the gaps between positive turning prevertices rule out $p \ge 4$ via comparison with the regular $(p+1)$-gon. Finite parameter ranges are certified using exact rational arithmetic and outward-rounded integer interval enclosures. In addition, we establish the sharp fourth-order asymptotic expansion of the spectral deficit at a prescribed positive-corner count, together with a quantitative local and global stability theorem for polygons with a large number of sides.

title: RightDiff: Learning Generative Reward Models to Judge by the Right Differences
authors: Qiyuan Chen, Hongsen Huang, Jiahe Chen, Renjie Hua, Hongxia Xu, Chuan Ren, Jian Wu
abstract: Generative reward models typically rely on generic query-level rubrics or unconstrained rationales, overlooking the fact that pairwise preference is driven by response-specific differences. Moreover, optimizing solely for outcome correctness encourages models to exploit superficial shortcuts such as verbosity and formatting, triggering rationale drift. To address this, we propose RightDiff, which structures pairwise evaluation into an evidence-grounded evaluation trajectory executed in a single autoregressive generation. RightDiff explicitly discovers contrastive differences between candidates, categorizes them into material or immaterial factors, and induces pair-specific rubrics before final adjudication. To train this process without post-hoc rationalization, we synthesize demonstration data via response-isolated prompts and optimize the reward model with a difference-alignment reward regularized by budget-constrained one-to-one matching and multiplicative gating. RightDiff achieves state-of-the-art preference modeling performance on RewardBench and RM-Bench, surpassing all open-source reward models and leading proprietary LLM judges. Downstream, it provides reliable supervision for direct preference optimization on Arena-Hard and AlpacaEval while effectively resisting length shortcuts.

title: Gaps between zeros of Epstein zeta-functions of binary quadratic forms on the critical line
authors: Stephan Baier, Srinivas Kotyada, Usha Keshav Sangale
abstract: We prove that for every integral binary quadratic form $Q$ whose discriminant is, up to sign, not a perfect square, the Epstein zeta-function of $Q$ has a zero $\frac12+iγ$ with $|γ-T|\le T^{2/5+ε}$ for all large $T$. For indefinite $Q$, that is, for zeta-functions of ideal classes of real quadratic orders, this is the first exponent below the classical barrier $1/2$. For positive definite $Q$ it improves the exponents $5/11$ of Jutila and Srinivas and $3/7$ of the authors, and for discriminant $-4m^2$ with $m$ odd we obtain $1/3$. A main ingredient, of independent interest, is an explicit Voronoi summation formula with additive twists to every modulus for the representation numbers of an indefinite binary form. The resulting dual sums are treated by a two-dimensional Weyl differencing, controlled by an exact formula for the Hessian determinant of the differenced phase.

title: ARS-VLM: Visually Aligned Augmented Random Search for Vision-Language Models
authors: Xiangwei Wang, Jianyuan Lin, Peng Wang, Saman Halgamuge
abstract: First-order reinforcement learning, such as Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), is widely used to post-train Vision-Language Models (VLMs) for multimodal reasoning. However, it incurs heavy memory and system overhead from backpropagation, optimizer states, and a reference model. Forward-only zeroth-order (ZO) methods, such as Evolution Strategies (ES) and its top-k variant Augmented Random Search (ARS), avoid these overheads via reward-guided weight perturbations, yet remain unexplored for VLM reasoning. We find that directly applying standard ES or vanilla ARS to VLMs suffers from two fundamental failure modes: (i) patch-grid overfitting, fitting fragile grid-specific visual token artifacts while ignoring spatial invariants, and (ii) catastrophic forgetting, degrading general perception and out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks due to unbounded high-rank parameter and policy drift. We propose ARS-VLM, a visually aligned Augmented Random Search framework for forward-only VLM post-training. First, ARS-VLM extracts a contrastive visual basis from bilinearly paired cross-grid views, concentrating perturbations on shared visual signals while suppressing patch-shift artifacts. Second, ARS-VLM anchors shallow visual-fusion layers with a soft subspace prior while freeing deep reasoning layers, restraining policy drift without a reference model. Third, ARS-VLM scores perturbations on paired views to discard view-fragile directions during top-k selection. We evaluate ARS-VLM on Qwen3-VL-4B and Qwen3-VL-8B on multimodal reasoning tasks. On 8B, ARS-VLM reaches 61.0% validation accuracy in 20 steps versus 150 for GRPO (7.5x fewer optimization steps) and avoids the late OOD collapse of vanilla ARS and ES. Moreover, ARS-VLM achieves 75.41% single-view micro accuracy across seven OOD vision reasoning benchmarks, compared with 75.31% for full-parameter GRPO, using forward-only post-training.
